question.problem:
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $4$ datapoints with $2$ features in the form of the $4\times 2$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0.866 & 1.212 \\ 0.866 & -0.173 \\ -0.866 & -1.212 \\ -0.866 & 0.173\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}0.670 & 0.224 & 0.224 & -0.671 \\ 0.224 & -0.671 & 0.671 & 0.224 \\ -0.670 & -0.224 & 0.224 & -0.671 \\ -0.224 & 0.671 & 0.671 & 0.224\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.191 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.095 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.707 & -0.707 \\ 0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following matrices corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance?

I. $[\begin{aligned}0.866 & 1.212\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.707 \\ 0.707\end{aligned}]$

II. $[\begin{aligned}0.866 & 1.212 \\ 0.866 & -0.173 \\ -0.866 & -1.212 \\ -0.866 & 0.173\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.707 \\ 0.707\end{aligned}]$

III. $[\begin{aligned}0.707 \\ 0.707\end{aligned}]$
question.worked_solution:
The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix ${X}^{T}X.$

Using the SVD and the fact that $U$ is orthogonal (i.e., ${U}^{T}U=I$), we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{T}X & =(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T}UΣ{V}^{T} \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}Σ{V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $Σ$ is a diagonal matrix, and so is ${Σ}^{T}Σ,$ we know that the eigenvectors of ${X}^{T}X$ are the columns of $V.$

In particular, the first principal component is the eigenvector of ${X}^{T}X$ corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. 
And since $Σ$ contains the corresponding singular values (square roots of the eigenvalues) in decreasing order, the first principal component is ${v}_{1},$ the first column of $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Option I represents the projection of only the first datapoint (the first row of $X$) onto the first principal component. Therefore, it produces a single scalar value rather than the full one-dimensional dataset.

- Option II corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Indeed, it represents $X\cdot {v}_{1},$ which is exactly the projection of the full dataset $X$ onto the first principal component.

- Option III represents ${v}_{1},$ which is the first principal component. It represents a direction in feature space, not a version of the data. Notice that it is also dimensionally incorrect, since it is a $2\times 1$ matrix instead of $4\times 1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
